newsitem.title: USA: NY precious metals end volatile day higher.
newsitem.headline: NY precious metals end volatile day higher.

text.p: New York precious metals futures ended a volatile day higher Thursday, led by silver, ahead of the December options expiries Friday.
But gold ended off the day's highs, as the U.S dollar found some support again late in the day, following an overnight plunge.

"Its all the fault of the Japanese, talking the dollar down and the yen back up, which created some nervousness in world financial markets, and resulted in some fund shortcovering in commodities, " Smith Barney Washington DC commodities strategist Phil Tiger said.
COMEX December gold ended up 90 cents at $379.60 an ounce, after seeing a six day high intraday at $382.00. Total gold futures volume was estimated at 55,000 lots.

Spot gold in the bullion market ended quoted $378.75/379.25 an ounce, compared to the London Thursday afternoon fix at $378.60, and the New York close Wednesday at $377.70/378.20. Intraday gold bullion recovered briefly to $381.00, after seeing a 19 month low at $376.80 last week.
COMEX December silver ended up 12.00 cents at $4.833 an ounce, after losing 8.000 cents Wednesday. Total silver futures estimated volume was 22,000 lots.
The bounce in silver followed a slide in spot silver in the bullion market to 18 month lows at $4.72 Wednesday.
The spot gold/silver ratio slumped to 78.22 at the close Thursday, after seeing a new 19 month high at 80.0 Wednesday.

The sharp fall in the dollar Thursday unnerved world stock and bond markets, but was seen beneficial for Asian demand for metals which had been depressed by the dollar's rise in the past year to 42 month highs.

Eisuke Sakakibara, director general of the Japanese Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau, said Thursday he thought the dollars correction from last year's sharp slide against the yen was about to end, and U.S. analysts suspect the Clinton administration's strong dollar policy may wane as the U.S. economy slows during Clinton's second term.
"It looks like, after more than two years, Japan has decided a weak yen is no longer in their economy's best interest," Tiger said.

"This does two things - it makes a stronger U.S. bond market questionable, with implications for equities markets, and makes commodities cheaper in domestic Asian currency terms, increasing demand for metals and grains," he said.
"But the CRB (Commodity Research Bureau) index hit 12 month lows last week and there is plenty of resistance above the market."
The CRB was up 1.75 points at 238.75 near the close Thursday.

Funds have been holding record net short open positions in gold futures recently, according to the CFTC Commitment of Traders reports, but open interest fell 4,259 lots in December gold Wednesday, as traders rolled positions into forward months, compressing the contango's, analysts said.
The December 1996/April 1997 gold spread ended steady Thursday though at $4.20 an ounce, after narrowing steadily in recent weeks.

"You had fund shortcovering and people trying to defend the $380 strike in December gold options which expire tomorrow, but the U.S. 30-year Treasury bond auction went OK, sending bond yields back down late in the day and the dollar recovered some ground near the close," Linnco Futures Group Chicago trader Anthony Raia said.
Open interest in December $380 put options outweighs open interest in the $380 calls by 6,296 lots to 1,107.

NYMEX January platinum ended up $3.40 an ounce at $386.30, after seeing a fresh life-of-contract low at $382.00 Wednesday, while NYMEX December palladium closed up $1.90 at $118.25 as platinum group metals bounced from technically oversold levels.
In the bullion market, platinum saw 35 month lows at $378.25 an ounce last Friday, while palladium saw 43 month lows at $114.00 last Thursday.
--Clive Mckeef, New York Commodities 212-859-1641; email: clive.mckeef@reuters.com
